text: Hi, guys.

text: My name's Ivan.

text: I'm on the Developer Experience team at Google DeepMind.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And today, we're covering the brand new Interactions API and our new offering, Managed Agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so to take a code from a very famous paper, an interaction is all you need.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Before we move on to what the Interactions API is and what the new Managed Agents offering is, let's take a trip down memory lane.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And let's kind of trace how models have changed and how we've worked with models.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So when we first started working with models, a lot of times you would have a single interaction.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You would send a message, tell me a joke.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then you might get a response.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For example, why don't scientists trust atoms?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Because they make up everything.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: After a while, as models got more and more capable, and they understood more about the world, this became a bit more complicated.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We wanted to take these models, put them in different applications.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But to do so, we needed them to be reliable.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so to do so, we invented function calling, where models could create
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Individual JSON objects with predictable structures.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Think like how when you want to register for a website, your web page sends a JSON payload to the back end with a username and a password, and that enables the back end server to say, OK, we have a new user, and now we can actually create a new account.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That made it possible for us to actually use models in different parts of this application, whether it's extracting user information, parsing data, and more.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But right now, we're seeing these incredible cups where models are getting more capable.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We're seeing models being able to reason, go for a very extended period of time before they come back to people.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so you're moving from a place where we went from completions
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Instruction and functions where we might ask, hey, what's the weather in New York City?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the model has a call weather tool that it can get the data, ingest it, and generate a response.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So now a case where models have multiple tools under their belt.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They're able to call tools, think and reflect on what the response meant, interact with the environment, and ultimately generate a response.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so this just brings us back to what is an agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Fundamentally, if you look at what an agent is, it's really a model that powers a huge chunk of it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A lot of people have reduced this to just a language model running in a loop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And for most cases, this is true.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you have a really capable model, you'll find that as we've got models that become more and more capable, a lot of the scaffolding has fallen away.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A lot of models, for example, the latest Opus models or Fable models, are now just immediately just using a bash tool instead of individually specialized tools like an edit file or a read file tool like we used to do.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so really what we have is a language model that's used to understand the context the user's intent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's given a bunch of different functions, all different resources that it then interacts with its environment in.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It has some short-term memory and some long-term memory to keep track of what it's encountered, and then an environment to execute functions in.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you're building a coding agent, but you don't give it an environment where it can actually execute code, for example, it's not going to be able to do anything.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So let's talk about the Interactions API now.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One of the things that we've seen, especially as we've moved from models to a dynamic where now we have models and agents, is that the kind of workloads that we want to support have changed significantly.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Through the Gemini API, you have Nano Banana, you have Gemini 3.5 Flash, but you also have very capable agents like the Deep Research agent that's going to run for anywhere from three minutes and more.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You interact with it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You have some sort of research plan.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's going to go out and do its own thing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it comes back with very deep and detailed research reports.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, it's pretty difficult then to think about consuming models and agents through a whole bunch of these different endpoints.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Additionally, for a lot of the older kind of API endpoints, a lot of the data was in very deeply nested objects.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so you can imagine the kind of difficulties that we had ourselves when we were building first party integrations.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we wanted these use cases where you might be able to generate a nano banana image, do some research, generate a VO image from there, or spawn out all these different agentic
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Kind of like agents that go out and do their own thing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so the Interactions API is our sort of solution to this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: As we look to build an API that can support all of these different use cases and ones that we can build on ourselves, if you look to bring Gemini across the entire surface of the Google ecosystem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the best place to get started is just with server-side state.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One of the things that you'll realize, especially if you use the new Gemini series of models, is that we essentially have this thing called thought signatures, where if you interact with the model, if it calls a function, if it gives a response, it's going to pass back a very opaque series of these numbers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For a lot of people, manually managing this was very difficult.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And sometimes when we talk to different startups, we found that they would lose their cash just with a single white space that they mistakenly added in.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So now with the responses API, you can see on the first turn, hi, my name is Phil.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And in the response, we give you a interaction ID.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And as long as you give us back that same interaction ID under the parameter previous interaction ID that you see in the second turn, all that context is preserved.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is really important with the new Gemini series of models because if you don't give us back those thought signatures, you're going to see a decrease in performance.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But what else does this unlock?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Here you see a demo built by Vamsi from our team.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They did an incredible demo where, using a single photo, you could generate with Nano Madonna all these different variations of yourself in different countries and different locations.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Each of these individual photos are a single interaction, but you can think of it from an initial API call.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It spawns all these different interaction calls.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Using those interactions, the same interaction ID, we then generate a video using the interaction ID and the new Omni model that we just launched.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Something like this would not have been possible without the Interactions API built by Philip over there.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So actually, it's a really incredible piece of work, I will say.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So to give you an example, an idea of what it would take to build something similar, this is all it would take.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First you pass in Gemini 3.1 flashlight image, generate an image of me in Venice.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You take the interaction ID, you chunk it back into the client.interactions.create, and this time you specify that you want the Omni flash model instead that we launched on Wednesday.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that allows you to now use the same Omni model with the same information, the same kind of images, and the same context throughout all these calls.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's making it possible to build more complex, rich, and just these very complex agentic applications.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The same thing occurs with audio generation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you look at the bottom, you see that now we have output.type.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In the past, you would have to take this very nested object, like .completions, .audio, and it would be very tricky for you to nest it out.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I can't even remember it off the top of my head.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But now every single bit of the outputs that come out are clearly demarcated by a strong type.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If it's an audio, as you see over here, all you've got to do is just parse it and handle it accordingly.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But what happens if now I want to generate an image?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's the same method over there, client.interactions.create.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: All you've got to do is just modify the response modality and the generation config.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And now I have an output.type of image.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this makes it very easy for me to start building and experimenting with Gemini.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The same thing comes with tool use.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can mix and match different inbuilt tools that wasn't possible before.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For example, over here, we're trying to get an agent to look up the internet to find the latest security reports for the React application.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We've given it access to the same index that Google has with type Google Search.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We've given it the ability to essentially retrieve information from web pages using the URL context tool that we ship with.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we've given it a custom tool here called File Incident.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The model can reason autonomously on its own, figure out what information it needs, and then actually generate a response to you all in a single API call.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This makes it very powerful, because now you have models that not only can work with information at the training cut of date, but beyond, because now they have access to the entirety of the internet.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And all this boils down to the new steps data model that we have, where instead of a world where we have a single message sent to a model and a response, we're going to have very complex things like async tool calls, models working together.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we want to make sure we have a strong data structure to support this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we've introduced the steps data model, which replaces the original legacy
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Outputs Array.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: With a type discriminator that makes it very clear at each step what the model output, what the dot signatures were, what the functions called were, and especially when it comes to the content that's being generated.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Earlier, you saw a content.type where it was audio and video.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this makes it easy to build these multimodal pipelines in a way that only the Gemini model families can.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The second thing that we've launched is anti-gravity as a remote agent, as what we like to call Manage Agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we've standardized around using the anti-gravity harness across all of our Google suite of products.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In AI Studio, which you saw just now, websites are built with the anti-gravity agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In the anti-gravity application, you're also using the anti-gravity agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now this is a very capable harness that we've co-trained Gemini on.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And moving forward, I think you're going to see many gains if you use this harness out of the box.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you wanted to build a coding agent in the past, you would first have to tune the harness.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then you have to find a sandbox provider, manage the infrastructure, and then kind of figure out a way how to preserve the context, especially in between runs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But with the anti-gravity managed agent, you get a persistent sandbox out of the box.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: With a single API call, you get a sandbox that you can keep hitting and treat as a personal claw without any sort of modifications.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can see an example over here where we want to analyze what's in a GitHub repository.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We then pass it over in an API call over to the anti-gravity agent, and it then boots up
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A remote sandbox and then starts investigating what the repository's about.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can see it calls a list file to get what's in the workspace.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It then reads each individual file.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then it generates a final report.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: All of this is happening in a remote sandbox without any sort of intervention from our site.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The agent's able to research, reason, and handle all of this autonomously.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We also handle multi-state persistent sandboxes, like what we mentioned earlier, where as long as you preserve the environment ID that will return to you, you're able to route it right back to the original sandbox that you had.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So these are two primitives that we've given you, the interaction.id, where you're able to preserve and work with context and ensure you're not busting your cache, and the environment ID that enables you to route it to the exact same context.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so this way, you can use the same sandbox.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You don't need to manage any sort of persistence of state.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And all you need to do is just add a few lines of code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The other way we've tried to make it easy is for you to be able to load in sources.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A lot of times you might have custom dependencies.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You might have .EMD files, helper files that you want to show on this specific sandbox.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The next question we often get from companies are, hey, I need my agent to be secure.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What am I going to do if my agent leaks a network credential?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And to do so, we've implemented a man in the middle proxy.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what does this mean?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A lot of times, you need to make API calls to different providers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Say, the Gemini API, you might need to download private GitHub repositories, et cetera.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have a proxy that stands in the middle.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so any call your model makes, we will look at the header, and we can replace items at will.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What you see over here is a case where we'll transform every single outbound call to the GitHub API and inject in the token dynamically.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so even if the model is somehow prompt injected and leaks your GitHub API token, it's never actually going to see the token.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's only going to execute code that will run against the GitHub API, and your token is never exposed.
